column1: What molecular mechanism allows two deposited layers to bond, and what thermal condition is required for it to occur?
column2: Polymer chain interdiffusion across the layer interface; the previous layer must still be above its glass transition temperature (Tg) when the next layer is deposited, otherwise molecular mobility halts and a weak mechanical boundary forms.

column1: What happens to a polymer's mechanical behavior below vs. above its glass transition temperature (Tg)?
column2: Below Tg: chains are locked in a rigid, brittle glassy state with only local bond vibration. Above Tg: chains gain segmental motion (backbone rotation and sliding), becoming rubbery/viscoelastic and capable of deformation without fracture.

column1: List the approximate Tg values for PLA, ABS, PA6 (nylon), and Polycarbonate.
What is the central invariant of filament geometry regarding diameter and volumetric flow?
column2: Volumetric flow is the conserved quantity the firmware/slicer relies on; diameter is the only input used to compute it. If actual diameter deviates from nominal, the volume calculation is wrong and errors propagate through layer height, extrusion width, and infill.

column1: Why is diameter oscillation (e.g., 1.72–1.78 mm averaging to 1.75 mm) worse than a consistent diameter offset?
column2: The oscillation itself is the defect—it creates rhythmic under- and over-extrusion, causing banding, weak layer bonds, and surface texture variation, even though the average diameter is correct.

column1: What are the typical dimensional tolerance tiers for 1.75 mm filament, and what do they represent?
column2: Premium filament: ±0.03 mm (~±1.7%); high-precision engineering grades: ±0.02 mm; commodity filament: ±0.05 mm. Tighter tolerance directly multiplies volumetric consistency and functional part accuracy.

column1: What causes thermoplastics used in FDM to be hygroscopic?
column2: Polar functional groups in the polymer chain structure (e.g., ester linkages in PLA) form hydrogen bonds with ambient water molecules, allowing moisture absorption.

column1: Why do standard PTFE-lined hotends impose a hard ceiling around 240°C?
column2: Beyond ~240°C, the PTFE liner degrades and releases toxic perfluoroisobutylene gas, making higher temperatures unsafe and damaging the liner.

column1: What advantage do all-metal hotends provide over PTFE-lined hotends, and what new risk do they introduce?
column2: All-metal hotends permit processing temperatures up to 300°C (enabling PC, nylon) via a low-thermal-conductivity heat break, but the expanded melt zone increases heat creep risk, which can soften filament prematurely and cause buckling during retraction.

column1: Explain the WLF (William-Landel-Ferry) relationship's practical implication for nozzle temperature tuning.
column2: Above Tg, viscosity decreases nonlinearly with temperature—small temperature changes cause disproportionately large viscosity shifts (e.g., a 10°C increase on nylon can drop viscosity 30–40%), explaining why small temperature tweaks can have outsized effects on flow and stringing.

column1: Why do semi-crystalline polymers (nylon, PP, PEEK, ABS) warp more than amorphous polymers (PLA, PETG)?
column2: Semi-crystalline polymers undergo sharp volumetric contraction as ordered crystalline domains form during cooling, creating differential shrinkage stress (outer perimeters cool/contract first while inner layers are pinned), causing curl and warp. Amorphous polymers solidify gradually without this ordered contraction.

column1: What three invariants govern advanced filament optimization according to the curriculum?
column2: 1) Melt rheology is nonlinear (WLF relationship). 2) Crystallinity governs both strength and warping. 3) Interlayer adhesion is determined by diffusion (time-and-temperature dependent chain interdiffusion), not just surface fusion.
